## What you will do

A **finfluencer twin** is a language model asked to answer as a particular
financial influencer would, given that person's public profile. The Talking to
Machines finfluencer panel interviews about 90 such twins every trading day and
asks each to rate 100 large US stocks. In this notebook you work with ten of
them:

1. **meet the twins:** read the profile card each twin is built from;
2. **see the interview:** the exact prompt the panel sends every day;
3. **interview a twin yourself:** once, live, on 20 stocks;
4. **open the archive:** the same ten twins' answers on the same 20 stocks over
   20 trading days, already collected;
5. **assemble a panel:** turn those answers into one bullish-or-bearish score per
   stock and day, the input Notebook 2 builds a trading signal from.

Only Section 3 calls a language model, and only if an API key is set. Everything
else runs offline.

**How to read this notebook.** As in Workshop 1, every table and figure the code
prints has a number, given in bold just above the code that prints it, and the
text says which table, row or column a number comes from.

The first block loads the R packages the notebook uses and sets the folders it
reads from and writes to.

```{r libs}
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
library(jsonlite)

DATA <- file.path("..", "data")
OUT  <- file.path("..", "output")
dir.create(OUT, showWarnings = FALSE)
```

---

## 1. The twins

Each twin starts from a **profile card**. In the panel itself the card is the
influencer's X profile (name, bio, follower counts, account age) followed by
their most recent posts. Here the cards are anonymous: the ten influencers are
`ff01` to `ff10`, their numbers are rounded, and their bio and recent posts are
described in a sentence or three rather than quoted.

The block below loads the ten cards as `cards` and prints who they are.

**Table 1.1.** `cards`: the ten twins.

```{r cards}
cards <- fread(file.path(DATA, "ff_persona_cards.csv"))
cards[, .(twin_id, on_x_since, followers, focus, audience)]
```

The next block defines `card_text()`, which writes one twin's card in the same
layout as the panel's profile block, and prints the card of the twin in `TWIN`.
Change `TWIN` to meet another one.

**Text 1.1.** The profile card of twin `TWIN`.

```{r card-text, comment = ""}
TWIN <- "ff05"

card_text <- function(id) {
  x <- cards[twin_id == id]
  paste0("- Profile ID: ", x$twin_id, "\n",
         "- Profile Description: ", x$bio, "\n",
         "- Profile Creation Date: ", x$on_x_since, "\n",
         "- Blue Verified Profile: ", x$paid_badge, "\n",
         "- Number of Followers: about ", format(x$followers, big.mark = ","), " Followers\n",
         "- Total Number of Tweets: about ", format(x$posts, big.mark = ","), "\n",
         "- Main focus: ", x$focus, "\n",
         "- Audience: ", x$audience, "\n",
         "- Recent posts (summarised):\n",
         paste0("  * ", strsplit(x$recent_posts, " | ", fixed = TRUE)[[1]], collapse = "\n"))
}
cat(card_text(TWIN))
```

---

## 2. The daily interview

Every trading day, each twin in the panel receives the same two messages:

- a **system prompt** that tells the model whose shoes to step into and pastes
  in the profile card;
- a **user prompt** with the rules of the survey, then one block per stock
  asking for a recommendation from 0 (a very strong sell) to 100 (a very strong
  buy), a confidence score, how speculative the answer is, an expected holding
  period, and the main catalyst.

The prompts below are the panel's own, from its public code repository. The block
loads them into `prompts` and prints where they come from.

**Text 1.2.** Source of the prompts.

```{r prompts, comment = ""}
prompts <- fromJSON(file.path(DATA, "ff_prompts.json"))
cat(prompts$source)
```

The panel's system prompt also invites the model to **search the web** for
up-to-date news about the stocks and themes the influencer cares about. That is
what keeps a twin current, and it is also what anchors each answer in time: a
twin interviewed on 3 September can find news up to 3 September and nothing
later. Notebook 2 relies on that. It tests whether a twin's view on day *t*
predicts returns *after* day *t*, which is only fair if the twin could not see
those returns.

The live interview in Section 3 has no web search, so the version used here
drops that paragraph. The block below prints the system prompt as your twin will
receive it.

**Text 1.3.** The system prompt, with twin `TWIN`'s card.

```{r system, comment = ""}
SYSTEM <- sub("{profile}", card_text(TWIN), prompts$system_workshop, fixed = TRUE)
cat(SYSTEM)
```

The next block builds the user prompt for the 20 stocks of this notebook. The
panel sends 50 stocks per message; 20 fit in one message comfortably. It prints
the rules, then the block for the first stock.

**Text 1.4.** The user prompt: the rules and the first stock's block.

```{r user, comment = ""}
slice <- fread(file.path(DATA, "ff_interviews_slice.csv"))
slice[, event_date := as.IDate(event_date)]
stocks <- unique(slice[, .(ticker, company)])[order(ticker)]
stocks[, label := sprintf("%s (%s)", company, ticker)]

blocks    <- vapply(stocks$label, function(s) sub("{stock}", s, prompts$stock_block, fixed = TRUE), "")
questions <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(stocks)), function(i)
  sub("{stock}", stocks$label[i], sub("{i}", i, prompts$stock_question, fixed = TRUE), fixed = TRUE), "")
USER <- paste0(prompts$user_prefix, paste(blocks, collapse = "\n\n"), prompts$must_answer,
               paste(questions, collapse = "\n\n"))
cat(prompts$user_prefix, blocks[1], sep = "")
```

The answer comes back as lines like `**recommendation: 70**`. The next block
defines `parse_answer()`, which turns that text into a table with one row per
stock. It prints nothing.

```{r parse-fn}
parse_answer <- function(txt) {
  parts <- strsplit(txt, "\\*\\*question:", perl = TRUE)[[1]][-1]
  field <- function(p, f) {
    m <- regmatches(p, regexpr(paste0("\\*\\*", f, ":\\s*([^*]*)\\*\\*"), p, perl = TRUE))
    if (!length(m)) return(NA_character_)
    trimws(sub(paste0("^\\*\\*", f, ":\\s*"), "", sub("\\*\\*$", "", m)))
  }
  rbindlist(lapply(parts, function(p) {
    q <- sub("\\*\\*.*$", "", p)
    data.table(ticker         = sub(".*\\(([A-Z.]+)\\)\\s*$", "\\1", trimws(q)),
               recommendation = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(field(p, "recommendation"))),
               confidence     = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(field(p, "confidence"))),
               speculation    = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(field(p, "speculation"))),
               holding_days   = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(field(p, "expected holding period"))),
               catalyst       = field(p, "primary catalyst type"),
               explanation    = field(p, "explanation"))
  }))
}
```

---

## 3. Interview a twin yourself

The next block sends the two prompts to the model once and parses the answer. It
uses the workshop key in your account; one interview costs well under one US
cent. The model is the one the panel uses. The answer is saved to `output/`, so
re-running the notebook does not ask again unless you change `TWIN` or delete the
file. With no key set, the block loads an interview that was run the same way
before the workshop, so the rest of the notebook still works.

**Text 1.5.** Where the answer came from.

```{r live, comment = ""}
MODEL   <- "gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07"
BASE    <- Sys.getenv("OPENAI_BASE_URL"); if (!nzchar(BASE)) BASE <- "https://api.openai.com/v1"
API_URL <- paste0(sub("/+$", "", BASE), "/chat/completions")
LIVE    <- file.path(OUT, sprintf("ff_live_%s.txt", TWIN))
EXAMPLE <- file.path(DATA, sprintf("ff_live_example_%s.txt", TWIN))

ask_twin <- function(system, user) {
  body <- list(model = MODEL, reasoning_effort = "low",
               messages = list(list(role = "system", content = system),
                               list(role = "user",   content = user)))
  resp <- httr2::request(API_URL) |>
    httr2::req_auth_bearer_token(Sys.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY")) |>
    httr2::req_body_json(body, auto_unbox = TRUE) |>
    httr2::req_retry(max_tries = 3) |>
    httr2::req_timeout(300) |>
    httr2::req_perform() |>
    httr2::resp_body_json()
  resp$choices[[1]]$message$content
}

if (!file.exists(LIVE) && nzchar(Sys.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"))) {
  writeLines(ask_twin(SYSTEM, USER), LIVE)
}
source_file <- if (file.exists(LIVE)) LIVE else if (file.exists(EXAMPLE)) EXAMPLE else NA
if (is.na(source_file)) {
  cat("No API key and no stored interview for", TWIN, "- Sections 3 and 5 are skipped.\n")
  mine <- data.table()
} else {
  cat("Answer read from", basename(source_file), "\n")
  mine <- parse_answer(paste(readLines(source_file, warn = FALSE), collapse = "\n"))
}
```

The block below prints your twin's answer, one row per stock, most bullish first.

**Table 1.2.** `mine`: your twin's recommendations today.

```{r mine, eval = nrow(mine) > 0}
mine[order(-recommendation), .(ticker, recommendation, confidence, speculation, holding_days, catalyst)]
```

The block below prints the twin's explanation for its most bullish stock, so you
can see how it argues from the card.

**Text 1.6.** Your twin's explanation for its top stock in Table 1.2.

```{r mine-why, eval = nrow(mine) > 0, comment = ""}
top <- mine[which.max(recommendation)]
cat(top$ticker, ":", strwrap(top$explanation, 90), sep = "\n")
```

## 4. The archive

The panel asked the same questions of the same ten twins every trading day. The
file loaded in Section 2 as `slice` holds their answers on these 20 stocks over
20 trading days, with the full profile card (including real posts) and web
search switched on. The block below prints its size.

**Table 1.3.** `slice`: twins, days, stocks and answers.

```{r slice}
complete <- slice[, .N, by = .(twin_id, event_date)][, sum(N == nrow(stocks))]
data.table(twins = uniqueN(slice$twin_id), days = uniqueN(slice$event_date),
           first_day = min(slice$event_date), last_day = max(slice$event_date),
           stocks = uniqueN(slice$ticker), answers = nrow(slice),
           twin_days_complete = complete, twin_days = uniqueN(slice[, .(twin_id, event_date)]))
```

A full grid would have 10 × 20 × 20 = 4,000 answers; Table 1.3, column
`answers`, is a little short of that, and `twin_days_complete` counts the
twin-days on which all 20 stocks were answered. The gaps are answers the panel
could not parse, a normal part of running a daily interview at scale.

The block below prints twin `TWIN`'s answers on the last day, with the reasons.

**Table 1.4.** Twin `TWIN` on the last day of the archive.

```{r slice-day}
last <- max(slice$event_date)
slice[twin_id == TWIN & event_date == last][order(-recommendation),
      .(ticker, recommendation, confidence, speculation, holding_days, catalyst)]
```

**Text 1.7.** Twin `TWIN`'s explanation for its top stock on that day.

```{r slice-why, comment = ""}
top_a <- slice[twin_id == TWIN & event_date == last][which.max(recommendation)]
cat(top_a$ticker, ":", strwrap(top_a$explanation, 90), sep = "\n")
```

---

## 5. Your interview against the archive

Your twin in Section 3 and the archive's twin share a name but not an input:
yours saw a short summary card and no news; the archive's saw the real posts and
searched the web that day. Figure 1.1 shows how much that matters. Each point is
one stock: across, the archive twin's average recommendation over the 20 days;
up, your twin's recommendation today. Points on the diagonal agree.

**Figure 1.1.** Your twin (Table 1.2) against the same twin in the archive.

```{r vs-archive, eval = nrow(mine) > 0}
arch <- slice[twin_id == TWIN, .(archive_mean = mean(recommendation, na.rm = TRUE)), by = ticker]
cmp <- merge(arch, mine[, .(ticker, yours = recommendation)], by = "ticker")
ggplot(cmp, aes(archive_mean, yours, label = ticker)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_text(size = 3.2) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "Archive twin: mean recommendation over 20 days", y = "Your twin: recommendation today") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

The block below puts one number on it: the correlation between the two columns
of Figure 1.1 across the 20 stocks.

**Table 1.5.** Agreement between your twin and the archive twin.

```{r vs-archive-n, eval = nrow(mine) > 0}
agree <- cmp[, .(stocks = .N,
                 correlation = if (uniqueN(yours) > 1) round(cor(archive_mean, yours), 2) else NA_real_,
                 mean_yours = round(mean(yours), 1), mean_archive = round(mean(archive_mean), 1))]
agree
if (is.na(agree$correlation))
  cat("Your twin gave every stock the same rating, so there is no correlation to compute.
")
```

A twin whose card says nothing about a stock has little to go on without news.
It answers 50, a hold, with a high `speculation` score; Table 1.2 shows both.
Some cards say nothing about most of these stocks: set `TWIN` to `ff01`, `ff06`
or `ff07` in Text 1.1 and every rating is 50, so Table 1.5 has no correlation.
At the other end, `ff08` and `ff10` follow their archive twins closely.

---

## 6. Assemble the panel

A single twin's rating is noisy. The panel's signal pools all twins: for each
stock and day, the share of twins rating it a **buy** (65 or more) minus the
share rating it a **sell** (35 or less). This is `net_buy_share`, from −1 (every
twin says sell) to +1 (every twin says buy). The block below computes it from
`slice` as a table called `mini_panel`, one row per stock and day, and prints its
size.

**Table 1.6.** `mini_panel`: stock-days, and twins per stock-day.

```{r mini-panel}
mini_panel <- slice[!is.na(recommendation),
                    .(n_twins = .N, mean_rec = mean(recommendation),
                      net_buy_share = mean(recommendation >= 65) - mean(recommendation <= 35)),
                    by = .(event_date, ticker)]
mini_panel[, .(stock_days = .N, median_twins = median(n_twins))]
```

Figure 1.2 shows who is bullish on what: each cell is one twin's average
recommendation for one stock over the 20 days, green above 50 and red below.

**Figure 1.2.** Average recommendation by twin and stock.

```{r heatmap, fig.height = 5}
hm <- slice[, .(mean_rec = mean(recommendation, na.rm = TRUE)), by = .(twin_id, ticker)]
ggplot(hm, aes(ticker, twin_id, fill = mean_rec)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#b2182b", mid = "white", high = "#1a9850", midpoint = 50,
                       limits = c(0, 100), name = "Mean\nrecommendation") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))
```

Ten twins are a small crowd. Notebook 2 uses the full panel: about 90 twins,
100 stocks and 52 trading days. The block below compares the two on the stocks
and days they share: how closely the ten-twin `net_buy_share` tracks the
full-panel one.

**Table 1.7.** Ten twins against the full panel, same stocks and days.

```{r vs-full}
full <- fread(file.path(DATA, "ff_signal_panel.csv"))[, event_date := as.IDate(event_date)]
both <- merge(mini_panel, full[, .(event_date, ticker, full_nbs = net_buy_share, full_twins = n_twins)],
              by = c("event_date", "ticker"))
both[, .(stock_days = .N, median_twins_here = median(n_twins), median_twins_full = median(full_twins),
         correlation = round(cor(net_buy_share, full_nbs), 2))]
```

Table 1.7, column `correlation`, says how much of the full panel's view ten
twins already capture. It flatters them a little: the ten are also among the
full panel's twins, so part of the agreement is the same answers counted twice.
The rest is what the other 80 or so add, and it is what Notebook 2 puts to the
test against returns.

## Exercises

**Exercise 1.1 — another twin.** Set `TWIN` to a twin whose focus in Table 1.1
differs from `ff05`'s (try `ff02` or `ff07`) and re-run Sections 1, 3 and 5. Is
it more or less bullish than `ff05`? Does it agree more or less with its archive
twin in Table 1.5?

**Exercise 1.2 — change the card.** Copy `card_text(TWIN)` into a string, edit it
(make the Tesla enthusiast `ff02` a Tesla sceptic, say), build `SYSTEM` from your
string, and call `ask_twin(SYSTEM, USER)`. How far does the recommendation for
TSLA move?

**Exercise 1.3 — the crowd's disagreement.** Using `slice`, find the stock on
which the ten twins disagree most (the largest standard deviation of
`recommendation` across twins, averaged over days). Does Figure 1.2 show why?

**Exercise 1.4 — confidence.** In `slice`, is a twin's `confidence` higher when
its recommendation is more extreme (far from 50)? Plot one against the other.

The block below saves `mini_panel` to `output/`, for your own use after the
workshop.

```{r save}
fwrite(mini_panel, file.path(OUT, "ff_mini_panel.csv"))
```
